# Comparing Initializations

The `S3` and `S3b` series only differed in how much energy was placed
into kinetic energy (KE) (the `b` version generated $2N$ random numbers
and then multiplied them by a factor to set the KE to the requested
target). The potential energy (PE) was always at its minimum. This
appears valid, as even in the transition region (`S3.00295` was
diffusing; see @fig-S3.295all).

```{r}
#| label: fig-S3.295all
#| fig-cap: "Plot of first execution of `S3.00295`. The KE and PE can be seen to settle down quickly."
S3.00295.0000 <- readplot( paste(td, "S3.00295.0000.scalars.csv", sep="/"))
```

The KE quickly (200 steps) gives up its initial value of 0.0264 to
settle around 0.013022, while it rings for a short while, by the end of
the first 1,000 steps it has settled down.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S3.295z
#| fig-cap: "Zoom into @fig-S3.295all.  The solid line is the final average of the run computed over 4,0999k steps (only the first 1k steps were skipped)."
plot(S3.00295.0000$ke[1:1000], typ="l", xlab="step", ylab="ke", 
     panel.first=grid())
abline(h=MD2DF.P[run=="S3.00295",ke.mean.rs])
```

## PE of a Single Particle

```{r}
#| include: false
 x<-MD2DF.P[run=="S3.00295", .(ke.mean.rs, steps.avg, total.steps, TE.mean.rs,
                               TE.sd.rs, TE.min.raw, TE.max.raw, pe.mean.rs)]
terng <- (x$TE.max.raw-x$TE.min.raw)/x$TE.mean.rs
```

Run `S3.00295` had a total per particle TE range (min to max) of
`r 100*terng`%. The average excess PE per particle (that is, the PE
above the minimum PE) is `r (pepp <- x$pe.mean.rs - 0.1159487884)` and
this is `r pepp/(terng*x$TE.mean.rs)` times the total TE range over 4M
steps. So while they are of the same order of magnitude, the per
particle share of that range is very small. The total available energy
is given by the KE of step zero, in which all of the added energy is
kinetic. This must be read from the text log, as the first step recorded
is the KE after the step. For this run, the value is 7.487, so the per
particle initialization KE is `r 7.487108031861905/256`, very close to
the desired initialization temperature of 0.0295 (which forms part of
the file name). The average excess PE of a single particle is therefore
`r 100 * pepp / (7.487108031861905 - pepp)`% of the total excess energy.

@fig-T410 shows the PE was clearly too high for the chosen temperature,
likely due to ignoring the positions of the particles when placing them:
particles randomly placed too close to each other will generate very
high energies. A "fudge factor" was introduced in version 1.3.5 which
altered the requested temperature for PE initialization. Using 0.5
(lowering the temperature by a factor of two) generated the following
results.

# Single Precision and Old Time Step

Series four will focus on the single precision (`Float32`) data and time
step of $\tau = 0.0177737$, which is close to what was used in 1979 (it
was somewhere between 0.0178315 and the above). The first step is to do
a `revtest()` with `Float32` and the higher time step. We choose to
initialize at a temperature of $T=0.03$ as it is hotter than we plan to
run.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
julia> julia> MD2.revtest( td, 30, "F320177.", 1000, T=Float32, tau=0.0177737)
temp = 0.03
basename = "/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/dev/testdata/
            F320177.0030"
---- initPE!: Temp = 0.015, a = 1.9046257
Linear Momentum: Float32[-0.024302304, 0.0051562395]
Corrected Linear Momentum: Float32[-3.434252f-9, 1.1641532f-10]
Angular Momentum: -11.559397
Moment of Inertia: 2786.8574
Corrected Angular Momentum: -5.722046e-6
Final Linear Momentum: Float32[2.6366324f-6, -3.6406913f-5]
-----saveMDRecord()
System state saved in /media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/dev/
testdata/F320177.0030.0000.jld2 at 2025-10-02T11:06:18.658
Current Steps: 0
Maximum Speed: 0.58966744)
RMS Particle Distance is 0.19545364, 
 10.262050577817634% of lattice spacing of 1.9046256137279147 
 
            Maximum delta was 0.7719284 on particle 211.

```

The final number is the sum of squared position errors. The RMS particle
error `r sqrt(12.138896/256)`, 11.4% of inter-particle distance, is
given by $\sqrt{\delta_i^2/N}$, where $\delta_i$ is the difference
between particle $i$'s position before and after moving 1,000 steps
forward and reverse, and $N$ is the number of particles. Here are some
example returns. @tbl-revtest shows the results.

| Name     | 64/32 | $\tau$    | RMS Dist. | \% Lattice | Max Part. |
|:---------|:-----:|:----------|:----------|:-----------|:----------|
| F64      |  64   | 0.01      | 0.0142    | 0.749      | 0.04169   |
| F64013   |  64   | 0.013     | 0.0366448 | 1.92       | 0.176     |
| F640177  |  64   | 0.0177737 | 0.14517   | 7.6218     | 0.37303   |
| F640177b |  64   | 0.0177737 | 0.14485   | 7.605      | 0.43965   |
| F640177c |  64   | 0.0177737 | 0.2774    | 14.5665    | 1.163     |
| F32      |  32   | 0.01      | 0.0170    | 0.89277    | 0.1067    |
| F32013   |  32   | 0.013     | 0.08027   | 4.215      | 0.2677    |
| F320177  |  32   | 0.0177737 | 0.19545   | 10.26      | 0.7719    |

: `revtest()` results for `Float64` and `Float32` and three different
time steps. Note that different runs can have different results. All
runs had an initialization temperature of $T=0.03$. {#tbl-revtest}

It is evident that the error is not sensitive to the precision, but very
sensitive to the time step. We also point out that a run with the larger
time step but an initialization temperature of $T=0.2$ had an RMS error
of 0.0357 which is 1.876% of the lattice spacing (less than a quarter of
that at the higher temperature).

`S4.0007` is oddly not valid at a temperature of 0.0079. Let's take a
closer look. We'll read it in separately and then plot it in @fig-S407.

```{r}
#| label: S407
S4.0007 <- combineruns( td, "S4","0007")
```

@fig-S407 is the plot of the current data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S407
#| fig-cap: HP plot of full series.  As of 9 October 2025, the series was not considered validly in equilibrium. The red line is the mean ke.
with( S4.0007$rundt, {HPplot( x=step*0.0177737, y=ke, typ="l", xlab="time", 
                              ylab="KE",panel.first=grid())})
abline( h = MD2DF.Q2[run=="S4.0007",ke.mean.rs],col='red')
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rm( S4.0007, S3.00295.0000, t4.0010.0000, t4.0010, t4b.0010.0000)
```

We will run more steps (so as this document is `knit`ted later it will
show a longer segment), but the estimate as of 10/9/25 is
$1.606\times10^{-8}$ (in units of the block average length of
`r with( MD2DF.Q2[run=="S4.0007"], steps.avg/nr)`), which over the full
length of the 1020k steps in the estimate (first 1k steps are skipped),
the temperature would rise only `r 1.606e-8 * 2040`.

Note that with a time step of 0.0177737, the `S3` series limit of 4M
steps at $\delta t = 0.01\tau$ (for a time of $t = 40,000\tau$) is the
equivalent of `2,250,516` steps (exactly), so we only need about 1.2M
more steps. In 50k step runs, We also need many more samples between
$T=0.010$ and 0.020.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pvskeS
#| fig-cap: Pressure vs temperature of series 4 in `MD2DF.Q2`.
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.Q2[series=="S4"], x="ke.mean.rs", y="Pressure", 
             xlab="temperature", ylab="pressure")
```

Since this will be necessary repeatedly, I changed the `runn()` code to
take an integer temperature that will be divided by 10,000 to make the
init temperature. Thus an input of 101 will init the temperature to
0.0101.

# Validity, Total Mometum, and Total Energy

There are a lot of colder runs not considered valid. We'll look at
`S4.00071`, which is initialized a scooch above `S4.0007` (also not
valid).

```{r}
#| label: S4071
S4.00071 <- combineruns( td, "S4","00071")
```

@fig-S4071 is the plot of the current data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S4071
#| fig-cap: Plot of TE of the full run of `S4.00071`.  As of 14 October 2025, the series was not considered validly in equilibrium. The red line is the mean TE, and the blue line the initialized TE.
with( S4.00071$rundt, {HPplot( x=step, y=TE, typ="l", xlab="time", 
                              ylab="TE",panel.first=grid())})
abline( h = MD2DF.Q6[ run=="S4.00071", TE.mean.rs],col='red')
abline( h = MD2DF.Q6[ run=="S4.00071", TE.init],col='darkblue')
```

@fig-TEM2Q6 plots the Maximum observed linear momentum squared ($M^2$)
plotted against the resampled TE variance (both of which which ought to
be small). The plot shows that for series 4 (black and red) all of the
non-valid points have higher TE standard deviation than the valid ones,
and most have a higher the usual maximum linear momentum. The series 3
have a scattering of of generally small values, but there is a cluster
of higher standard deviation TEs in series 3 that are all not valid.
This is concerning, as TE and momentum growth is a symptom of the
simulation not obeying two basic conservation laws (i.e., the simulation
is broken).

```{r}
#| include: false
rm( S4.00071)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-TEM2Q6
#| fig-cap: Maximum of the momentum squared vs. TE standard deviation. Green squares and magenta inverted triangles are valid and not-valid Series 3, black circles and red triangles are series 4. 
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.Q6[series=="S4"], y="M.2.max.raw", x="TE.sd.rs", 
             xlab="TE SD", ylab="Max M^2", linethresh=200, log = 'xy', 
             xlim = c(2e-7,3e-4), ylim = c(1e-9, 1))
with( MD2DF.Q6[grepl( "S3", series)], {
      col = ifelse( valid, 'darkgreen', 'magenta')
      pch = ifelse( valid, 0, 6)
      points( x = TE.sd.rs, y = M.2.max.raw, col = col, pch = pch)
      })
```

The absolute growth of the TE (the maximum observed TE across all steps
minus the initialized TE) should be most sensitive to things going
amiss.

```{r}
#| label: fig-TEMTESDQ6
#| fig-cap: Growth of TE (i.e., `TE.max.raw - TE.init`) vs. the TE standard deviation. Green squares and magenta inverted triangles are valid and not-valid Series 3, black circles and red triangles are series 4. 
with( MD2DF.Q6[series=="S4"], {
      col = ifelse( valid, 'black', 'darkred')
      pch = ifelse( valid, 1, 2)
      plot( y=TE.max.raw - TE.init, x=TE.sd.rs, pch = pch, col = col,
            xlab="TE SD", ylab="Energy", log = 'xy', panel.first = grid(),
            xlim = c(2e-7,3e-4), ylim = c(1e-8, 0.001), 
            main = "Growth of TE vs TE sd")
      })
with( MD2DF.Q6[grepl( "S3", series)], {
      col = ifelse( valid, 'darkgreen', 'magenta')
      pch = ifelse( valid, 0, 6)
      points( y=TE.max.raw - TE.init, x=TE.sd.rs, col = col, pch = pch)
      })
```

It is possible that this is simply related to the mean TE.

Since most of the not-valid samples are very long runs, it is not
immediately worrying that there is energy growth, but let's examine it
in more detail.

## Validity Regressions

We can look for correlations systematically. Below we create a series
item labeled `s2` from the first two characters of the `series` column
(thus `S3b` is grouped with `S3`), lp for the log of the total momentum
squared, and one labeled `TEd` that is the logarithm of the maximum
energy delta. We'll create a copy of the `Q6` database with just the
data in which we are interested.

```{r}
#| label: Q6lm
Q6lm <- copy( MD2DF.Q6[ grepl( "S[34]", series), 
                     .(valid, TE.mean.rs, TE.sd.rs, lts = log( total.steps),
                       TEd = {TEd0 = TE.max.raw - TE.init;
                                     ifelse( TEd0 <= 0, 1e-11,  log( TEd0))},
                       lp = log( M.2.max.raw), s2 = substr( series, 1, 2))])
```

We've looked at correlations with KE, `psiavg`, and `psiabs`, and found
none. So below we look at all combinations of series, valid, total
momentum squared, and log of total steps. We purposely leave out the TE
standard deviation as we already know it has a linear relationship to
energy growth (see @fig-TEMTESDQ6).

```{r}
#| label: TElm
TElm <- lm( TEd ~ valid * s2 * lts * lp, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm)
```

Lots of significance (F-statistic p-value \< $2\times 10^{-16}$), but
difficult to interpret. The `model.matrix( TElm)` function can help to
understand what each term means. @fig-TEMTESDQ6 shows that series 4 has
a much higher energy growth than series 3. Since large numbers of steps
are due to being in the transition region and thus the system not being
in stable equilibrium, we drop `lts`, and look at `valid` and `s2` only.

```{r}
#| label: TElm2
TElm2 <- lm( TEd ~  valid * s2 , data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm2)
```

The four coefficients in order are $\alpha_i$ for $i$ in {0, 1, 2, 3}
for the following equation:
$y = \alpha_0 + v \alpha_1 + S_4 \alpha_2 + v S_4 \alpha_3$, where $v$
is one if valid and $S_4$ is a one if it is series 4 (both zero
otherwise). For not valid series 3, $v$ and $S_4$ are both zero, and
only the intercept ($\alpha_0$) is left. The variance of this intercept
is based on the whole data set though, and since the series 4 data
energy growth is over 20 times the series 3, that dominates the
variance. Valid series 3 data has $v=1$, but since $S_4=0$, the valid
series 3 energy growth is estimated to be $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1$, and
this is the expected small number ($\ln(\delta E) \approx -13$, so
$\delta E \approx. 2.3 \times 10^{-6}$. $\alpha_2$ estimates the
not-valid series 4 growth. Below are the predictions for the four cases.

```{r}
(pTElm2 <- predict( TElm2, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"))))
```

Basically, the not-valid series 3 energy growth is pretty small. The
estimate for not-valid series 4 is $\alpha_0 +\alpha_2$. Valid series 4
is almost significant at the 5% level, and the estimate is the sum of
all four coefficients..

Below we look at series 3 alone, and we can see that the not-valid data
has a significantly different energy growth, but that total steps is
very significant.

```{r}
#| label: TElm3
TElm3 <- lm( TEd ~  valid * lts,  data = Q6lm[  grepl( "S3", s2),])
summary( TElm3)
```

The low $r^2$ indicates that it doe not explain the results. The `lts`
coefficient is significant at the 5% level, but there is no significance
to the `valid:lts` pair, meaning that there really isn't extra growth
with validity (or non-validity). Below are the coefficients for the
various conditions.

```{r}
(pTElm3 <- predict( TElm3, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"),
                                     lts = rep.int(0,4))))
```

We can look at a simpler example of `valid`, `s2`, and `lts` for the
whoe dataset:

```{r}
#| label: TElm4
TElm4 <- lm( TEd ~  valid + s2 + lts, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm4)
```

Here, log of steps are significant. The equation for this model is
$y = \alpha_0 + v \alpha_1, + S_4 \alpha_2 + \alpha_3 \ln(n)$ (where $n$
is steps). $\alpha_{0-2}$ define intercepts for the varias cases of
valid and series.Vvalid series 3 intercept is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1$,
not-valid series 4 is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_2$, and valid series 4 the sum
of all three coefficients. Below we see that the valid series 3
intercept shows a negative energy growth (`lts` $= 0$ is the equivalent
of `total.steps` $\approx 3$).

```{r}
(pTElm4 <- predict(TElm4, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"),
                                     lts = rep.int(0,4))))
```

Below we try valid and valid:series 4:

```{r}
#| label: TElm5
TElm5 <- lm( TEd ~  valid/s2, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm5)
```

Everything is significant, but $r^2$ is small. The model here is
$y = \alpha_0 + v \alpha_1 + v S_4 \alpha_3$. So, the intercept
($\alpha_0$) is the `!valid` case and covers both `S3` and `S4`. Valid
series 3 is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1$. Below are predictions from the above
for the four cases of `!valid` / `valid` and `S3` / `S4`.

```{r}
(pTElm5 <- predict(TElm5, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"))))
```

Adding in log of maximum of total momentum squared to the regressions
(see @fig-TEM2Q6):

```{r}
#| label: TElm6
TElm6 <- lm( TEd ~ valid + s2 + lp, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm6)
```

The model is
$y = \alpha_0 + v \alpha_1 + S_4 \alpha_2 + \alpha_3 \ln (p^2)$ (where
$p$ is the total momentum). So momentum is a useless predictor of energy
growth. As before, the intercept alone is the intercept for not-valid
series 3. Valid series 3 intercept is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1$ (and
negative), not-valid series 4 intercept is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_2$, and
valid series 4 intercept is $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$.

```{r}
(pTElm6 <- predict(TElm6, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"),
                                     lp = rep(0, 4))))
```

Let's add total steps and TE mean back in.

```{r}
#| label: TElm7
TElm7 <- lm( TEd ~ valid + s2 + TE.mean.rs + lts + lp, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm7)
```

Another low $r^2$, and momentum, mean TE and valid state show no
significance next to series and the log of total steps.

The following will remove the intercept, and estimate a coefficient for
the log of total steps.

```{r}
#| label: TElm8
TElm8 <- lm( TEd ~ valid:s2 + lts:s2 - 1, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm8)
```

A high $r^2$. We basically estimate separate intercepts for each series,
but, while each is significant, they are not significantly different
from each other. The model formula is
$y = (\alpha_{0,S3}v + \alpha_{1,S3} \ln(n))S_3 + (\alpha_{0,S4}v + \alpha_{1,S4} \ln(n))S_4$,
essentially an equation for each series. The below will show the four
possibilities at 2M total steps, along with th 95% confidence interval
for those predictions.

```{r}
(pTElm8 <- predict(TElm6, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"),
                                     lp = rep(log(2e6), 4)), 
                   interval = "confidence"))
```

We can see that the series 3 predictions overlap, perhaps barely, but
definitely.

A similar regression with the formula `TEd ~ valid + lts:s2 - 1` gives
essentially the same answer, but with a zero intercept for With eight
models, let's complete our decent into `lm` hell using `step()`:

```{r}
#| label: TElm9
TElm9 <- lm( TEd ~ valid + lts:s2 - 1, data = Q6lm)
summary( TElm8)
```

```{r}
(pTElm9 <- predict(TElm6, newdata = data.frame( 
                                     row.names = c("!vS3","!vS4","vS3","vS4"),
                                     valid = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                                     s2 = c("S3","S4","S3","S4"),
                                     lp = rep(log(2e6), 4)), 
                   interval = "confidence"))
```

```{r}
#| label: TElmstep
TElm10 <- step( TElm7, trace = 0)
TElm11 <- step( TElm, trace = 0) 
```

We'll look at the AIC's to see which fit was best.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-TElmAIC
#| tbl-cap: AIC results for all previous linear models across both series 3 and 4.
knitr::kable( AIC( TElm, TElm2, TElm4, TElm5, TElm6, TElm7, TElm8, TElm9, 
                   TElm10, TElm11))
```

`TElm10` is the best:

```{r}
summary( TElm10)
```

This "best" estimate has a low $r^2$ and shows significance for total
energy and steps.

What did we learn? There is no compelling case that there is energy
growth for not-valid runs. Energy growth does depend on number of steps
and total energy, but this is expected. The series 4 growth is
concerning though, and we will have to look at improvements in the
*Julia* code.

## Validity Change with Diffusion Calculation

It is also evident that a lot of the heating and cooling groups had been
considered valid, then diffusion runs were made, and were no longer
considered valid. @tbl-S3nv shows a list of `S#` runs that were once
valid, but became not-valid after the diffusion runs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-S3nv
#| tbl-cap: The `S3` runs with less than 1M steps and no longer valid.  Since all runs under 4M steps were valid before diffusion runs, these runs became invalid after thier diffusion runs.

knitr::kable(MD2DF.Q6[ grepl( "S3", series) & !valid & steps.avg < 1e6, 
          .(run, ke.mean.rs, steps.avg, total.steps)])
```

Here is one of the higher energy runs.

```{r}
#| label: S309h17
#| fig-cap: Run `S3.0009h17` kinestic energy with resampled points overplotted. Note that the `HPplot()` plotting function resamples the data differently than `rsmpavg()`, so the overlay is imperfect.

S3.0009h17 <- combineruns( td, "S3","0009h17")
HPplot( S3.0009h17$rundt$ke, typ='l', panel.first = grid())
abline( h = MD2DF.Q6[ run=="S3.0009h17",ke.mean.rs], col='red')
S3.0009h17rske <- rsmpavg( S3.0009h17$rundt$ke, 500)
points( x = 500 * seq_along( S3.0009h17rske), y = S3.0009h17rske,
        col='green')
```

That sort of looks like bad luck. There were
`r (ns3d <- MD2DF.Q6[ grepl( "S3", series) & steps.avg < 1e6 & !is.na(nrd), .N])`
runs with less than 1M steps made
`r (ns3dv <- MD2DF.Q6[ grepl( "S3", series) & valid & steps.avg < 1e6 & !is.na(nrd), .N])`
remained valid and
`r (ns3nv <- MD2DF.Q6[ grepl( "S3", series) & !valid & steps.avg < 1e6, .N])`
switched to not-valid. This is a ratio of `r 100 * ns3nv / ns3d`%;
compare this to the empirically derived 14.4% estimated from 10,000
50-sample normally distributed sequences.

```{r}
#| include: false
rm( S3.0009h17, S3.0009h17rske)
```

# Pressure

The pressure is given by the equation:

$$
\langle P \rangle = \rho \left( T + \frac{n \left< U \right>}{2N}\right)
$$

where $\rho$ is the density, $T$ is the temperature, $n$ is the exponent
of the potential energy, $N$ is the number of particles, $U$ is the
total potential energy, and the brackets indicate averages. This can be
simplified to
$\langle P \rangle = \rho (T + \frac{1}{2}n\left< u \right>$ where we
let $u$ be the per particle potential energy. The assertion is that
thermal energy will be shared equally among all accessible states, and
thus the excess potential energy (that is, the per-particle potential
energy less the minimum per-particle potential energy) will roughly
equal the kinetic energy. The minimum PE is 0.1159487884. @fig-Press
below shows how the actual pressure compares to that predicted by equal
excess potential energy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Press
#| fig-cap: Pressure versus temperature for series 3 and 4. Blue line is the pressure that one would expect if the excess potential energy per particle were equal to the kinetic energy.
with( MD2DF.Q6[ !grepl( "S2", series) & ke.mean.rs < 0.021,], {
      plotconf( y = Pressure.mean.rs, x = ke.mean.rs, Fval = Fval, 
                panel.first = grid(), linethresh = 400,
                xlab = "T", ylab = "P")
      eppe <- ke.mean.rs + 0.1159487884 # accessible states PE
      peppe <- (1/pi) * ( ke.mean.rs + 5 * eppe / 2)
      lines( x = ke.mean.rs, y = peppe, typ='l', col = 'blue')
      
      })
```
